title: Inspect who experiences the errors
summary: Use subgroup metrics carefully and avoid conclusions from tiny samples.

sections.title: An average can hide unequal behavior
paragraphs: A model may have similar overall accuracy while missing many more positive cases in one subgroup. Compare metrics relevant to the application, such as false-negative rates, false-positive rates, and calibration, rather than selecting only the most flattering summary.

Choose slices for a reason grounded in how the system is used. Data collection and labels may already contain inequities. Model evaluation cannot repair those assumptions by itself, and adding a sensitive attribute requires a legitimate purpose and careful handling.

sections.title: Numbers need context
paragraphs: Small subgroup counts produce unstable estimates. Report the numerator and denominator and investigate representative failures. Do not rank groups or claim a systematic disparity from a handful of toy observations.

Fairness definitions can conflict when base rates differ. There is no single universal metric that settles every application. Document the intended use, affected people, acceptable trade-offs, and a review process.

code.source:
rows = [("a", 1, 1), ("a", 1, 0), ("a", 0, 0),
        ("b", 1, 1), ("b", 1, 1), ("b", 0, 1)]
for group in ["a", "b"]:
    positives = [(y, p) for g, y, p in rows if g == group and y == 1]
    missed = sum(p == 0 for _, p in positives)
    print(group, {"missed_positives": missed, "actual_positives": len(positives),
                  "false_negative_rate": missed/len(positives) if positives else None})
code.explanation: Groups a and b are synthetic placeholders. Two positive examples per group are far too few for a reliable real-world conclusion.

steps: Calculate each group’s false-positive count and negative count.
Write one sentence explaining the sample-size limitation.
practice.solution: Group a has no false positives among one negative; group b has one among one negative. These rates are extremely unstable. Report the counts and request more representative evidence before making a deployment claim.
practice.expected: The toy false-negative rates are 0.5 for a and 0 for b, based on two positives each.

quiz.question: Why might equal accuracy be insufficient?
options: Different kinds of errors can affect groups differently
Every subgroup must have identical examples
quiz.explanation: The distribution and consequences of errors matter, not only the total number correct.
